query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticle structural and chemical stability at high temperatures is governed by the persistence of a locally ordered short‐range atomic arrangement that limits atomic diffusion and suppresses phase segregation, thereby stabilizing the single-phase, near-equiatomic structure under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized via physical or chemical routes with nominally single-phase, homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Application of in-situ high-temperature environmental TEM combined with X-ray scattering during heating (800–1200 K) under controlled reactive gas atmospheres to directly monitor local compositional order and morphological evolution.
generation.conditions: High-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operation conditions, with a focus on the catalytic regime (800–1200 K) under controlled atmospheres ensuring low noble-metal content.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local short-range atomic ordering that modulates elemental diffusion and suppresses the onset of phase separation or nanoparticle coarsening.
generation.mechanism: Persistent short-range order reduces the thermodynamic driving force and kinetic pathways for elemental segregation. This atomic arrangement impedes rapid diffusion at elevated temperatures, thereby maintaining the single-phase, near-equiatomic state. In contrast, nanoparticles lacking this ordering would exhibit enhanced diffusion leading to phase separation and morphological instability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles showing strong local short-range order will display minimal compositional segregation and preserve their morphology under in-situ high-temperature reactive conditions relative to baseline nanoparticles (with weaker order or more compositional fluctuations) that will exhibit measurable phase separation or coarsening.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced via less controlled fabrication processes, which result in a more random atomic distribution and lower initial short-range order.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature regimes relevant for catalytic (around 773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (up to ~1923 K) applications, particularly when the material has a near-equiatomic composition with low noble-metal content. It may not extend to nanoparticles with substantially different size distributions or impurities that override the effects of short-range ordering.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the relative contributions of nanoparticle size distribution and slight compositional deviations on the observed stability, which may also influence diffusion kinetics and ordering phenomena.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one set through a controlled synthesis method known to induce high short-range order and a second set via a method that promotes random atomic distributions. Subject both sets to in-situ high-temperature environmental TEM and X-ray scattering under identical reactive gas atmospheres (800–1200 K). Monitor real-time compositional mapping, morphological evolution, and phase changes over extended dwell times.
measurements: Atomic-scale compositional maps using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX).
Diffraction patterns for detecting phase segregation or coarsening.
Time-resolved imaging to capture morphological changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with initially high short-range order show similar rates of elemental segregation, phase separation, or morphological degradation as those with random distributions under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that local ordering is the governing factor in stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. decision.trend: Early work (PMC4999872, 2016) on AlxCoCrFeNi revealed that near-equiatomic single-phase regions can exhibit enhanced radiation tolerance due to sluggish diffusion, energizing efforts to exploit high configurational entropy for stability under extreme conditions. Creep studies on CoCrFeNiMn alloys (PMC7512559, 2018) showed that although these alloys can deform at 500–600 °C with dynamic microstructural evolution, the interplay between multi-element composition and structural stability at elevated temperatures remains complex. Powder-metallurgy fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr (PMC6926650, 2019) highlighted how processing routes shape microstructure and impurity content, but persistent questions remain about their high-temperature phase stability and chemical homogeneity. Subsequent work on 3D-printed HfNbTaTiZr for extreme environments (PMC11077685, 2024) demonstrated oxidation resistance improvements via tailored processing, yet the mechanistic underpinnings of how complex solid-solution compositions resist phase separation still lack clarity. Meanwhile, Monte Carlo simulations (PMC11375216, 2024) established that short-range chemical order modestly enhances lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr, hinting that local arrangement might underlie both mechanical and chemical stability. Nevertheless, direct links between compositional fluctuations, service conditions, and the emergent stabilities in multi-element nanoparticles have yet to be conclusively determined.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether subtle local orders or phase-separation tendencies ultimately govern the high-temperature structural and chemical robustness of multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles. Current studies establish that these alloys can form nominally single-phase structures and can exhibit beneficial high-temperature properties, yet no definitive mechanism explains how local clustering, surface segregation, or complex diffusion pathways impact long-term morphological stability and catalytic or thermoelectric performance under operating conditions (473–1923 K). Differences in fabrication route, nanoparticle size distribution, and partial pressure of reactive gases all introduce uncertainties that hamper a full mechanistic understanding of stability drivers.
decision.lever: High-temperature in-situ environmental TEM and X-ray scattering on size-controlled nanoparticles at 800–1200 K under controlled reactive gas atmospheres, coupled with compositional mapping to track real-time interdiffusion and morphological evolution.
decision.why: Given emerging evidence that short-range ordering, local composition fluctuations, and distinct diffusion pathways may underpin high-temperature stability, an in-situ approach directly probing nanoparticles under realistic catalytic or thermoelectric conditions will discriminate among proposed mechanisms. If local atomic arrangements mitigate diffusion and stabilize the near-equiatomic solid solution, then real-time imaging and spectroscopic data will show minimal compositional segregation and stable morphology relative to a baseline reference with less compositional complexity. If, however, the key factor is relentless phase separation kinetics, the experiment will reveal precipitate formation or nanoparticle coarsening. Such direct observation provides a clear falsification test for competing hypotheses on how element distribution and synthesis–structure–property relations impart high-temperature resilience.
